rv.q: Arch, introspective, and also about a guy who sadistically murders homeless people, it’s as singular as anything Goold ever staged here, and a worthy bookend to the greatest London artistic directorship of recent times.
It doesn’t look or sound like any other musical you'll see in London, and there’s something entrancing about this icy injection of nihilism into a remorselessly peppy genre.
By turns devastating and quick-witted, scintillating yet unexpectedly moving, the piece raises all sorts of hopes for Goold's embyronic Almeida tenure.
Goold’s direction is sophisticated; he accentuates the aesthetic materialism of the story, establishing this solid sense of unease from the very start.

A musical still needs good tunes to work, and Duncan Sheik’s offerings are, for the most part, bang on the money: synth-laden earworms peppered with re-arranged covers of ’80s’ classics, the music acts like an intoxicating insight into the fractured prism of Bateman’s mind.
The ensemble cast delivers strongly throughout and exudes confidence.

cn.t: Goold's musical adaptation of Ellis's capitalist critique earns strong praise as a standout achievement in a crowded musical theater season, with its sell-out success cementing its status as a fitting highlight.
